newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian minister seeks rational LPG pricing.
newsitem.headline: Indian minister seeks rational LPG pricing.

text.p: India needs to closely examine the heavily-subsidised price of domestic liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) supplies as demand balloons, Petroleum Minister Janeshwar Mishra said on Thursday.
"The time has come when we need to take a closer look at the choice between providing more LPG and a more rational pricing for it," Mishra told a meeting of parliament deputies.
The minister said rational pricing of LPG was of great significance since most of its users were from the better-off sections of society.

He said domestic LPG was heavily subsidised and its increased usage would lead to an even higher subsidy bill. The administered LPG price, exclusive of excise duty, is 6,901.95 rupees per tonne against an import-parity price of 21,066 rupees per tonne.
Although the customer population for LPG has gone up to 29.3 million on March 31, 1997 from 16.98 million on March 31, 1991, there are 14.1 million customers on the waiting list.
The Petroleum Ministry plans to release an additional four million LPG connections during 1997/98 ending March 31.
Mishra also stressed the need for rationalising the prices of other petroleum products affecting the national economy due to the rising share of imports in total oil consumption.
Crude oil and petroleum product imports have risen to 336.57 billion rupees during 1996/97 from 97.74 billion rupees in 1990/91, he said.

"The oil pool deficit, which was 57 billion rupees on March 31, 1996 had risen to 155 billion rupees by March 1997. In the absence of remedial measures, the deficit is expected to rise to about 245 billion rupees by the end of the current financial year (March 31, 1998)," Mishra said.
"Correct pricing of petroleum products also needs to be looked into to avoid their wasteful use and adulteration."

The oil pool deficit, which represents the money owed by the government to oil companies for selling petroleum products below market prices to support India's subsidy regime, is estimated to currently total 190 billion rupees.

Mishra said the government was discussing the deficit problem with political parties to arrive at a solution, adding that uncertainty over the pricing policy was affecting the liquidity position of oil companies as well as the inflow of new investments into the sector.

Non-payment of dues from the pool account has put Madras Refineries Limited and Cochin Refineries Ltd under severe strain, Mishra said. Other oil firms like Bharat Petroleum Corp Ltd and Hindustan Petroleum Corp Ltd were also facing problems, the minister said.

The managers of Indian Oil Corp's planned $350 million global depository receipt (GDR) issue have indicated that the liquidity crisis in the country's biggest state-owned oil firm was a cause for serious concern among global investors, he added.
Mishra said that given the large scale investment required to meet the projected demand for petroleum products, policy changes were essential to provide energy security.
"It is essential to reform the system so that such situations do not arise at all in future and potential investors are provided a stable policy regime free from uncertainty."
